notes: IMPORTANT: a finding's `line` is the SINK CALL site for a DFA rule, and the ANNOTATION site for an AST rule. The manifest lines below are the measured lines.
This category covers three framework shapes that a scanner meets when it is run WITHOUT the project's dependency jars -- the normal situation for a source-only scan.

SHAPE 1 (Spring JDBC, DFA): the receiver type cannot be resolved, so the TAC writes the callee signature with a SIMPLE receiver name ('JdbcTemplate.query/2') rather than a fully qualified one. Every sink pattern is anchored to a fully qualified name, so before the sink matcher learned to accept the simple-name form, none of these sinks was reachable and no error was raised. The 'dfa-taint-sql-injection' findings below are the evidence that the pattern now matches.

SHAPE 2 (MyBatis / Spring Data, AST): the TAC does not carry annotations and a mapper method lowers to a bare RETURN, so the taint engine cannot see a '${}' placeholder. This detection is therefore an AST rule, 'ast-security-orm-sql-interpolation'.

SHAPE 3 (framework entry points, DFA): a Spring controller has no 'getParameter()' call anywhere -- the framework binds the request value to the method parameter BY ANNOTATION. The taint engine therefore treats a parameter carrying @RequestParam / @PathVariable / @QueryParam as a source whose origin is the HTTP request, and the finding names that origin ('param:customer@spring-mvc:RequestParam'). The 'TP-framework-entry-point' case is the one where the sink is in the SAME method, so the source label is visible in the finding itself; the cross-file cases are attributed to the sink, the same way category 01 is.

SHAPE 4 (Quarkus REST and Micronaut, DFA): the same entry-point model, but each framework names its binding annotations differently. Quarkus uses @RestQuery / @RestHeader / @RestCookie; Micronaut uses @QueryValue / @Header / @Body. Micronaut's names were entirely missing from the taint engine's list, which instead held 'HeaderValue' and 'PathValue' -- names no framework defines -- so a value from a Micronaut request reached the SQL sink with no taint flow to follow. The trust boundary is identified by the BINDING annotation, not the endpoint annotation: Quarkus REST shares @Path and @GET with JAX-RS, so the endpoint annotation alone cannot tell them apart, but @RestQuery versus @QueryParam can.

SHAPE 5 (request beans, DFA): a CONTAINER annotation (@RestBeanParam, @BeanParam, @RequestBean) does not bind a value -- it binds a bean OF values, and the binding annotation sits on the bean's FIELD. The bean class declares no method and no initializer, so it produced NO function in the IR and its @RestQuery was invisible: the value that reached the sink had no framework origin to name. The TAC now records every declared class's field annotations, and the finding names the FIELD and the field's own annotation ('param:params.customer@quarkus-rest:RestQuery'). The container parameter itself is a CARRIER, not a source: it is labelled 'param:params@carrier', so a field the framework did not bind is not reported as a framework entry point.

The two ORM placeholder forms have opposite safety semantics: '#{name}' becomes a PreparedStatement placeholder and the value is bound as DATA; '${name}' is a raw string substitution and the value becomes part of the SQL TEXT. Only the raw form is reported.

A '${}' that names something the method does not receive is not a finding: a dynamic table name or column is a legitimate use of raw substitution, because a prepared-statement placeholder cannot stand in for SQL structure.
The style findings on these fixtures are NOT part of this category. The category scores the two framework rules; the style noise is measured by the style categories.

cases.note: Spring JDBC queryForList with the tainted customer name concatenated into the SQL text. The receiver is an unresolved third-party type, so the IR writes 'JdbcTemplate.queryForList/1'.

The same shape through JdbcTemplate.query rather than queryForList. The sink matcher must not treat 'query' as matching 'queryForList' -- these are two different methods, and each is pinned separately.
A tainted value reaches a write statement through JdbcTemplate.update. The statement is an UPDATE with two tainted parameters.

The named-parameter template variant. The receiver simple name is 'NamedParameterJdbcTemplate', so this case proves the relaxed sink pattern matches the SIMPLE NAME of the receiver, not only the class named in the pattern.

A Spring @RequestParam bound parameter reaching the SQL sink IN THE SAME METHOD. There is no getParameter() call anywhere in this file -- the framework binds the value by annotation -- so the source is the parameter annotation, not a call. The finding's source is 'param:customer@spring-mvc:RequestParam': it names the trust boundary rather than an opaque parameter. The label is ASSERTED, not assumed: a model that produced the right number of findings with a bare parameter label would fail this case.

A Quarkus @RestQuery bound parameter reaching the SQL sink in the same method. The source is 'param:customer@quarkus-rest:RestQuery'. Quarkus REST uses the JAX-RS ENDPOINT annotations (@Path on the class, @GET on the method), so the endpoint annotation alone cannot identify it -- but the BINDING annotation can, and the finding names Quarkus rather than JAX-RS. The label is ASSERTED, so a model that attributed this to jax-rs would fail here.

A Micronaut @QueryValue bound parameter reaching the SQL sink in the same method. The source is 'param:customer@micronaut:QueryValue'. Micronaut names its binding annotations differently from every other framework, and the taint engine's list used to contain 'HeaderValue' and 'PathValue' -- names no framework defines -- while the real @QueryValue was missing. The label is ASSERTED.

A Quarkus resource method that takes a request value without Bean Validation. Before the shared annotation catalogue the validation checker knew thirteen binding annotations and the taint engine knew twenty-six, so a @RestQuery parameter was tracked as attacker-controlled by one layer and treated as trusted-by-default by the other -- and this rule never fired.

A Micronaut controller method that takes a request value without Bean Validation. Micronaut's @QueryValue was invisible to the validation checker before the shared catalogue, so no CWE-20 finding was raised for a Micronaut application at all.
MyBatis @Select with a raw '${name}' substitution. The placeholder names the method's own parameter, so the caller controls the SQL text.
MyBatis @Update with a raw '${name}' substitution, mixed with a bound '#{id}'. The two placeholder forms in one statement must be told apart: only the raw one is reported.
MyBatis @Delete with a raw '${name}' substitution.
MyBatis @Insert with a raw '${name}' substitution.

PRECISION PROBE: the customer name is passed as a bound parameter to a '?' placeholder, so it cannot change the statement. The same receiver and the same method name as TP-jdbc-query-for-list, so this case fails if the matcher only looks at the call shape.
PRECISION PROBE: the tainted value is only logged; it never reaches a SQL sink. System.out.println is not a CWE-89 sink.

PRECISION PROBE for the framework entry-point model: a @RequestParam parameter is labelled as a request-bound value, but it only reaches a log call. A model that tainted every value a request touches would report here. The line is the call site of the log-only repository method; the finding, if there were one, would be attributed to the sink in OrderRepository.

A plain parameter with NO binding annotation reaches the same sink in the same class. It IS reported -- a plain parameter is an ordinary taint source -- so this is a true positive, not a false positive. Its value is as a LABEL probe: the source must stay 'param:customer' and must NOT acquire a framework qualifier. The assertion is on the whole 'taint: param:customer ->' head, so a source of 'param:customer@quarkus-rest:RestQuery' would NOT satisfy it. The trust boundary comes from the binding annotation, so a parameter without one carries none, even in a Quarkus resource.

The Micronaut counterpart of TP-quarkus-plain-parameter: reported, and the source stays a bare parameter with no framework qualifier. Without this control, a model that labelled EVERY parameter of a framework class would produce the right number of findings here while producing the WRONG source label, which is what a reader of the report actually sees.
PRECISION PROBE: a @RestCookie parameter is labelled as a request-bound value, but it only reaches a log call. A model that tainted every value a request touches would report here.

A @RestBeanParam request bean's FIELD reaching the SQL sink in the same method. The container annotation names the BEAN; the binding annotation sits on the FIELD, so the source must name the field and the field's own annotation: 'param:params.customer@quarkus-rest:RestQuery'. Before the field-level model the bean class produced no function in the IR at all -- it declares no method and no initializer -- so its @RestQuery was invisible and the finding named an opaque parameter instead. The label is ASSERTED, so an implementation that attributed this to the container ('param:params@quarkus-rest:RestBeanParam') would fail here.

A second bound field of the SAME bean. The resolution is per FIELD, not per bean: the field name comes from the FIELDLOAD and the annotation from that field's own declaration. Without this case an implementation that always picked the bean's FIRST bound field would pass the previous one.

A field the framework did NOT bind ('internalNote' carries no binding annotation). It IS reported -- it is a value derived from a request-supplied bean -- but the source must be the CARRIER label 'param:params@carrier', not a framework entry point. Claiming a framework origin here would be a false claim: no annotation bound that field. The assertion is on the whole head, so 'param:params.customer@quarkus-rest:RestQuery' would NOT satisfy it. Without this case, a model that attributed every field of a container-bound bean to the framework would pass the two cases above.

PRECISION PROBE for the request-bean model: a bound field ('params.customer') that only reaches a log call. The field IS a framework entry point, but it never reaches a SQL sink. A model that reported every field of every request bean would report here. The line is the call site of the log; the finding, if there were one, would be attributed to the sink.
PRECISION PROBE: '#{name}' is a bound parameter. The value is bound as data and cannot change the statement. Reporting it would be a false positive on the single most common MyBatis placeholder form.
PRECISION PROBE: '${tableName}' names a table the method does not receive, so the caller cannot influence it. A dynamic table name is a legitimate use of raw substitution.
PRECISION PROBE: a bound '#{name}' in an @Insert.
